meaning: Each tie is a pointer that landed. Whether the paper and the Lean say the same thing is a reading.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal statement gives every language in NP one polynomial-time verifier with logarithmic randomness, a constant proof-bit query bound, perfect completeness and soundness error $1/2$, as the surrounding paragraph asserts.
rows.name: PCP.np_subset_pcp
rows.annotation: The witness checker in the opening is the input to `np_subset_pcp`. The constructed verifier works for the whole language, and the proof whose bits it reads may be a new encoding of the witness.

assessments.fidelity_note: The formal statement supplies the verifier promised here: exactly $\alpha\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil+\beta$ fair bits, at most $\ell$ proof queries below $p(n)$, perfect completeness and soundness error $1/2$. The quoted introduction needs the following bullets to display those guarantees.

The formal statement supplies one polynomial-time verifier and constants for the whole language, with the exact randomness, query, proof-length, completeness and soundness bounds listed immediately after the quote. This is the same source span as the earlier theorem passage.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal statement supplies the verifier promised here: exactly $\alpha\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil+\beta$ fair bits, at most $\ell$ proof queries below $p(n)$, perfect completeness and soundness error $1/2$. The quoted introduction needs the following bullets to display those guarantees.
rows.name: PCP.np_subset_pcp
rows.annotation: `V.queries = q` fixes a constant upper bound on the depth of the adaptive query tree. `ReadsBelow` supplies a different bound, on how far into the proof any branch can read even when each branch reads only a few bits.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal statement puts the language in NP for the same concrete machine model, assuming a polynomial-time verifier, exact logarithmic randomness, a polynomial proof-address bound, perfect completeness and soundness error $1/2$. These are the properties assumed in the paragraph.
rows.name: PCP.pcp_subset_np_concrete
rows.annotation: The accessible proof prefix is the NP witness, and the random seeds are enumerated by the deterministic checker. Because the verifier uses logarithmically many bits, the number of seeds is polynomial. Soundness ensures that each guessed prefix for a no-input has a rejecting run.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal statement equates the two grid-vanishing conditions with the cubic vertex and edge equations. In the characteristic-two field containing $\mathbb F_4$ fixed in Section 4, those equations are exactly the proper-colouring conditions established just before the quote; the adjacency factor removes nonedges.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.ThreeColorGrid.constraints_iff_satisfies
rows.annotation: `Satisfies` contains the vertex and edge cube equations for the evaluations of one fixed polynomial. On the grid, $E$ is the adjacency indicator. The identification with three colours uses the field calculation preceding the passage.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal statement says that the graph is three-colourable exactly when some polynomial of degree at most $(|H|-1)m$ makes both $\operatorname{Val}$ and $\operatorname{Prop}$ vanish on the grid, in characteristic two with a primitive cube root of unity. The quote is the pointwise statement for a given $\chi$; this is its consequence for solvability.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.ThreeColorGrid.colorable_iff_exists_constraints
rows.annotation: The existence claim adds a degree ceiling to the fixed-polynomial argument. Starting from a colouring, interpolation bounds the degree in each coordinate by $|H|-1$. Starting from a witness polynomial, restriction to the grid gives the colouring.

rows.fidelity_note: The quoted sentence gives a decomposition for a polynomial vanishing on a finite grid over a field. The formal statement proves both directions, supplies degree bounds on the coefficient polynomials, and works over any integral domain.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.GridVanishing.vanishesOn_iff_exists_decomposition
rows.annotation: Each summand contains a coordinate factor that vanishes on the grid, giving the reverse implication immediately. The forward implication removes terms by monic division and uses uniqueness of the low-degree remainder. Those steps work over an integral domain.

rows.fidelity_note: For a polynomial vanishing on the grid, the formal statement gives quotients $Q_j$ with $P=\sum_j Z_H(X_j)Q_j$ and $\deg Q_j+h\leq\deg P$ for every nonzero $Q_j$, as the quote says. It works over any integral domain, not only a field.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.GridVanishing.exists_decomposition
rows.annotation: In the division step, cancelling a term of degree at most $\deg P$ with a monic degree-$h$ factor contributes a quotient term of degree at most $\deg P-h$. The formal bound excludes zero quotients because their `totalDegree` is defined as zero.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal statement gives the stated $2\delta$ distance under $q\geq10^6d^3$ and $\delta\leq1/(4\cdot10^6)$, with the comparison parameter uniform over the whole field. It applies in every finite-field characteristic, beyond the characteristic-two setting fixed in Section 4.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.PointLineTest.exists_close_of_small_rejection
rows.annotation: The small disagreement is measured with a uniform parameter on an indexed line. Even if different indices of the same geometric line supply inconsistent polynomials, the theorem recovers one nearby polynomial on the point domain under the stated field-size bound.

rows.fidelity_note: The quote asserts both set-multilinearity and a degree bound. The formal statement gives the first part: every monomial of the encoded polynomial uses exactly one variable from each digit group. It holds for every input polynomial; the degree bound is the other cited statement.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.SetMultilinear.encode_isSetMultilinear
rows.annotation: `IsSetMultilinear` is a condition on monomials in the support. Each supported monomial chooses exactly one variable from each digit group. A zero coefficient leaves no monomial to check.

rows.fidelity_note: The quote asserts both set-multilinearity and a degree bound. The formal statement gives the degree bound $c$; the one-variable-per-group condition is the other cited statement. The degree bound also holds without the restriction $j<b^c$ on the input degree.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.SetMultilinear.totalDegree_encode_le
rows.annotation: There are $c$ groups, so each monomial contributed by the encoder has degree $c$, and the resulting polynomial has total degree at most $c$. The input-degree restriction is needed for exact recovery under substitution.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal definition assigns $z^{jb^i}$ to the coordinate for digit position $i$ and digit value $j$. In particular, every coordinate with $j=0$ equals one even at $z=0$.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.SetMultilinear.evaluationPoint
rows.annotation: The coordinate exponent is the contribution of digit $j$ in position $i$ to the represented exponent. For $j=0$ this contribution vanishes, so the coordinate is one even at $z=0$.

rows.fidelity_note: For positive base $b$ and degree strictly below $b^c$, the formal statement gives $\widetilde p(\Phi(z))=p(z)$ at every $z$, including zero. It also works over any commutative semiring, whereas the exposition uses a field; the preceding construction supplies the degree restriction.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.SetMultilinear.eval_encode
rows.annotation: Substituting the digit powers adds their exponents, which recovers every exponent of $p$ strictly below $b^c$. This explains both the cutoff and the identity at zero. Lean needs only a commutative semiring for the calculation.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal statement gives the stated $2\delta$ distance under $q>2c$ and $\delta<1/[2(c+2)^2]$. It also applies to finite fields of arbitrary characteristic, whereas the exposition has fixed characteristic two since Section 4.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.GeneratorLowDegreeTest.exists_close
rows.annotation: The node condition uses successive powers of a generator, with Lagrange weights for evaluation at zero. The strict rejection threshold is used in proving that plurality correction gives an exact solution of the interpolation test. The conclusion concerns existence over any finite field.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal definition evaluates the binary dot product of the message and the requested homogeneous linear label. This is precisely $h_s(x)=s\cdot x$ over $\mathbb F_2$.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.Hadamard.linearEncode
rows.annotation: `linearEncode` adds the label’s coordinates with weights given by the message. Since this is a linear map of the label, the difference of its values at $R+L$ and $R$ gives its value at $L$, the identity used for a masked read.

rows.fidelity_note: For any two distinct binary messages, the formal statement says their homogeneous linear encodings have relative distance exactly $1/2$. This is the distance claim justified in the quote by pairing zeros and ones.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.Hadamard.relativeDistance_linearEncode
rows.annotation: For distinct messages their difference has a nonzero coordinate. Translating the label by that coordinate vector swaps the agreement and disagreement sets, giving exactly half the labels in each.

rows.fidelity_note: If BLR rejection is at most $\varepsilon$, the formal statement supplies a binary linear functional at distance at most $\varepsilon$ from the word. There is no small-error hypothesis.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.BLR.exists_linearMap_distance_le_of_rejection_le
rows.annotation: BLR estimates distance to a linear map on the label space. A linear map can still send the constant label to the wrong bit or fail to respect label products, which is why the Hadamard test adds checks for those properties.

rows.fidelity_note: For label degree $r\geq1$, rejection at most $\delta<1/28$ gives one message whose encoding is within $\delta$ on all degree-at-most-$r$ labels and within $3\delta$ on all affine labels. Both distances refer to that same message.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.Hadamard.test_soundness
rows.annotation: The same message supplies the two distance bounds. Affine consistency is a separate test because for cubic labels the affine subspace can be a tiny fraction of the full label space.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal statement gives exactly $2r+4$ positions in the test's query list, which is ten for the degree-three test with $r=3$, as the quote says.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.Hadamard.testQueries_length
rows.annotation: The query list has length $2r+4$ for every seed. Length counts repeated positions too, so the result gives a bound on reads even when a particular seed requests the same address more than once.

ties.name: PCP.Algebraic.ThreeColorVerifier.Proof
ties.plain: Four points and four lines tables

rows.fidelity_note: The formal definition supplies exactly four points tables and four encoded lines tables. The colour and difference points tables use degree-three labels, the two certificate points tables use affine labels, and all four lines tables use affine labels.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.ThreeColorVerifier.Proof
rows.plain: Four points and four lines tables
rows.annotation: The fields of `Proof` allow arbitrary received bits. The colour and difference tables have cubic labels to support the derived cubic checks, and the affine labels on the certificate and line tables suffice for their linear tests and correction.

ties.name: PCP.Algebraic.EncodedLineLowDegreeTest.exists_close
ties.plain: One polynomial for both label domains

rows.fidelity_note: The formal statement supplies one polynomial of degree at most $D=cb^c$ within $S\kappa$ on both full and homogeneous linear labels, as claimed. It also permits $c=0$ under the same node conditions, whereas the exposition fixes positive $c$; the second distance is not over all affine labels.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.EncodedLineLowDegreeTest.exists_close
rows.plain: One polynomial for both label domains
rows.annotation: With $J\kappa$ below the point-versus-line threshold, a single decoded polynomial gives both conclusions. Full-label distance controls masked reads of composed labels, and distance on homogeneous linear labels controls the linear comparisons.

ties.name: PCP.Algebraic.BinaryLocalCorrection.run
ties.plain: Reject or return a corrected bit

rows.fidelity_note: After its inner test and nonzero-parameter comparison pass, the formal definition returns the correction at $\Phi(0)$. It reuses exactly the same inner slope and homogeneous label for the comparison and return.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.BinaryLocalCorrection.run
rows.plain: Reject or return a corrected bit
rows.annotation: The inner test and the comparison at the sampled nonzero parameter must both pass before `run` returns the bit at $\Phi(0)$. The same slope and label can be used at the two inner targets because the error estimate bounds the chance of either prediction failing.

ties.name: PCP.Algebraic.BinaryLocalCorrection.run_eval
ties.plain: Honest tables give the requested bit

rows.fidelity_note: In characteristic two, with distinct test nodes and valid correction nodes, the formal statement says that honest points and lines tables of a polynomial $P$ of degree below $b^c$ make the corrector return the bit $L(P(a))$ for every slope, nonzero $z$, label and inner seed, never a rejection.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.BinaryLocalCorrection.run_eval
rows.plain: Honest tables give the requested bit
rows.annotation: Exact encoding recovery applies because the honest restriction has degree strictly below $b^c$. Both inner corrections then agree with polynomial evaluation for every seed, so the sample-point comparison passes and the returned bit is the homogeneous observation at $a$.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal statement assumes $q>2c$, generator nodes for the test and the correction, and a polynomial $P$ of degree at most $D$ whose encoding is within homogeneous distance $\delta$ of the points table, with any lines table. It bounds the probability of rejection or a wrong returned bit by $C\kappa_a+\delta+D/(2(q-1))$, averaged over all the corrector's random choices, including the homogeneous label.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.BinaryLocalCorrection.failure_le
rows.annotation: `failure_le` compares the output to `some` of the right bit at the fixed target. Its rejection term is local to that target. The global distance estimate applies to the comparison at a nonzero line parameter, where a uniform slope makes the point uniform.

rows.fidelity_note: The quote first describes rejection by an ideal polynomial test. The formal statement instead bounds rejection of the actual two-corrector test after allowing errors in nearby polynomial encodings; its lower bound depends on $D$, $h$, $q$, both distances and the correction constant.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.BinaryZeroOnGridCorrection.rejectionRate_ge
rows.annotation: `rejectionRate_ge` concerns the received tables. The ideal-polynomial rejection is used as a lower bound before subtracting the chances that the primary table or either of the two certificate corrections supplies a bad bit.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal definition gives the four low-degree checks, two grid checks and difference check individually. It evaluates one selected check; requiring all seven to pass is a separate formal definition.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.ThreeColorVerifier.branchTest
rows.annotation: `branchTest` takes one of seven indices and a seed of the corresponding type. In particular, the certificate grid tests can have a different seed shape from the low-degree checks.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal definition accepts exactly when all seven specified checks accept. Through their definitions, these are the four binary low-degree tests, two zero-on-grid tests and difference consistency check listed in the quote.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.ThreeColorVerifier.test
rows.annotation: `test` evaluates the conjunction of the seven branch verdicts. The event that a given branch rejects is contained in the event that this conjunction rejects.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal definition gives the vertex grid check's corrector the entries of the vertex-certificate lines table from the received proof, the same table that the binary low-degree test on that certificate reads.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.ThreeColorVerifier.validAuxiliary
rows.annotation: `validAuxiliary` indexes the existing vertex-certificate lines table by target and slope. Reusing it adds no proof table, and each call still checks the entry it reads before returning a correction.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal definition gives the edge grid check's corrector the entries of the edge-certificate lines table from the received proof, the same table that the binary low-degree test on that certificate reads.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.ThreeColorVerifier.properAuxiliary
rows.annotation: `properAuxiliary` uses the existing edge-certificate lines table after the pair of vertex coordinates is flattened. The different point type accounts for the two vertices and the certificate coordinates without introducing another table.

rows.fidelity_note: With distinct test nodes, valid correction nodes, the three field colours, nonempty $H$ and $5m(h-1)<b^c$, the formal statement gives a proof with rejection probability zero for every three-colourable grid graph. Uniform sampling from a finite seed space makes this acceptance for every seed.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.ThreeColorVerifier.exists_proof_rejectionRate_eq_zero
rows.annotation: The proof is chosen before the seed. The $5m(h-1)$ bound puts the honest certificate degrees below the digit cutoff, and the honest-evaluation lemmas then give zero rejection on the finite seed space.

rows.fidelity_note: For every proof and each of the seven checks, the formal statement bounds that check's rejection probability by the rejection rate of the whole seven-check verifier, with no factor of seven, as the quote says.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.ThreeColorVerifier.branchRejectionRate_le
rows.annotation: The full seed projects to a uniform seed for any one branch. A rejection in that branch is contained in the full rejection event, so the bound needs no factor for the number of branches.

rows.fidelity_note: For the construction's parameters, the formal statement rejects every proof of a non-three-colourable graph with probability at least $g(c)$. It assumes $q\geq10^6D^3$, $100Dh\leq q$ and $m(h-1)\leq D$, with the stated characteristic-two field and interpolation nodes; Appendix A supplies these conditions.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.ThreeColorVerifier.rejectionRate_ge_of_not_colorable
rows.annotation: If rejection is below the gap, the low-degree branches first give four nearby polynomials. The remaining checks force the two vanishing identities and the consistency of the difference polynomial, so those polynomials yield a colouring. The field and degree comparisons in the statement are needed to make the error bounds smaller than the ideal rejection bounds.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal statement establishes polynomial running time for the step algorithm of the implemented amplified graph verifier on a concrete machine model. Together with its fixed query bound, this supplies the polynomial-time verifier described here.
rows.name: PCP.Lang.ThreeColorRuntime.polyTimeAlg
rows.annotation: `polyTimeAlg` is a machine-level running-time bound for producing the queries and acceptance data of the amplified verifier. Counting the proof bits read would leave open the time required to compute their addresses.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal statement bounds the bits read by the seven checks, for every seed, by $2c+18$, $2c+14$, $2c+18$, $2c+14$, $6c+20$, $6c+20$ and $3$, in the quoted order. At $c=4$ these are $26,22,26,22,44,44$ and $3$.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.ThreeColorVerifier.branchQueries_length_le
rows.annotation: `branchQueries_length_le` bounds the length of the selected branch’s query list for every seed. The two low-degree branches with cubic labels use longer lists than the ones with affine labels, and the grid checks each include two correction calls.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal statement bounds the bits read by one run of the seven-check verifier, for every seed, by $20c+107$, which is $187$ at $c=4$. It is an upper bound, so some seeds may read fewer bits.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.ThreeColorVerifier.queries_length_le
rows.annotation: The full list concatenates the seven branch lists, so summing their uniform bounds gives $20c+107$. At $c=4$ this gives the single-run upper bound of $187$ reads used before repetition.

rows.fidelity_note: The quote gives an unamplified rejection gap and a numerical repetition count. The formal statement gives the amplified verifier's $187R$ query bound, exact logarithmic randomness, polynomial proof bound, perfect completeness and soundness error $1/2$; it does not state the two displayed numerical equalities.
rows.name: PCP.Algebraic.ThreeColorAmplifiedVerifier.verification_guarantees
rows.annotation: The formal clause gives the query and seed budgets in terms of $R$, with soundness $1/2$ after repetition. The numerical single-run gap is established in the fair-bit sampling analysis.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal definition supplies clauses enforcing $z_0=0$, each update $z_{i+1}=z_i\lor(x_i\mathbin{\mathrm{xor}}p_i)$, and $R(p)\lor z_k=1$. It does this for every input pattern and every supplied relation, padding shorter clauses with false.
rows.name: PCP.Reduction.FiniteBooleanConstraints.clauses
rows.annotation: The flags track whether the current input has differed from a fixed pattern so far. If it matches the pattern, the last flag is zero and the final clause requires the relation at that pattern. Short clauses are padded with false literals.

rows.fidelity_note: The formal statement proves that all three displayed clauses hold exactly when $z=u\lor v$. The first two clauses are represented with an additional false literal, which leaves their truth values unchanged.
rows.name: PCP.Reduction.FiniteBooleanConstraints.orGate_iff
rows.annotation: The first two clauses require $z$ when either input is true. The third requires at least one true input whenever $z$ is true. Together they enforce the OR update for each flag.

topics.description: Polynomial-time verification with logarithmic randomness and a constant number of proof-bit queries characterizes NP.
topics.name: PCP theorem

topics.description: A language belongs to NP when membership is witnessed by a polynomial-length string accepted by a polynomial-time checker.
topics.name: NP witness verification

topics.description: Accepting computations become finite constraints, Boolean clauses and graphs while preserving the existence of a witness.
topics.name: Reduction to three-colouring

topics.description: The Schwartz–Zippel bound limits the fraction of points where a nonzero polynomial vanishes.
topics.name: Polynomial distance

topics.description: Interpolation represents a table on a grid by a unique polynomial with a degree bound in each variable.
topics.name: Low-degree extension

topics.description: A polynomial vanishing on a grid admits a decomposition using the coordinate vanishing polynomials and a certificate expressed by two identities.
topics.name: Vanishing certificates

topics.description: Vertex values and edge differences satisfy polynomial equations exactly when they define a proper three-colouring.
topics.name: Colouring constraints

topics.description: Four pairs of points and lines tables supply the answers read by four low-degree tests, two grid tests and a difference check.
topics.name: Proof tables and checks

topics.description: An honest colouring passes every check, while sufficiently small rejection forces four nearby polynomials to describe a proper colouring.
topics.name: Completeness and soundness

topics.description: Corrected certificate queries test vanishing identities at prescribed points and relate failure on the grid to rejection.
topics.name: Zero-on-grid test

topics.description: Random line queries recover a polynomial value at a prescribed point or bound the probability of accepting a wrong value.
topics.name: Local correction over fields

topics.description: Weighted bit queries and tests of encoded line entries recover a homogeneous observation at a prescribed point, allowing rejection.
topics.name: Local correction on bits

topics.description: Small rejection gives one polynomial whose encoding is close to the points table on both full and homogeneous labels.
topics.name: Binary low-degree test

topics.description: A random choice between Hadamard testing and a binary weighted identity tests one encoded line entry for low degree.
topics.name: Inner low-degree test

topics.description: Writing exponents in a fixed number of base digits replaces a line polynomial by a polynomial of fixed total degree.
topics.name: Set-multilinear encoding

topics.description: Agreement with supplied line polynomials at random points yields one nearby polynomial of bounded total degree.
topics.name: Point-versus-line test

topics.description: Weighted interpolation at generator powers tests low degree, with plurality correction turning small rejection into polynomial agreement.
topics.name: Standard low-degree test

topics.description: Agreement between low-degree row and column polynomials produces a nearby bivariate polynomial and consistent values at selected crossings.
topics.name: Bivariate agreement

topics.description: Polynomial labels turn field values and their polynomial expressions into bits and distinguish full, affine and homogeneous observations.
topics.name: Labels and encoding

topics.description: Linearity, unit, product and affine consistency checks test whether a word is close to the encoding of one field value.
topics.name: Hadamard test

topics.description: Linearity testing finds a nearby linear word, and two randomly shifted queries recover a requested value with controlled error.
topics.name: Linearity and self-correction

topics.description: A finite multi-stack machine implements the verifier or witness checker with polynomial running time.
topics.name: Polynomial-time implementation

topics.description: A verifier selects an adaptive query tree from its input and random seed, with explicit acceptance probabilities and proof-address bounds.
topics.name: Verifier and query trees

topics.description: Query counts, fair-bit sampling, proof length and independent repetition give the resource bounds and final soundness error.
